subject: language_arts

unit.title: Spelling with suffixes
unit.essentialQuestion: How do I add an ending to a word so it's still spelled correctly?

title: Double the consonant (run → running)
objectives: By the end, I can double the final consonant of a short-vowel word before a vowel suffix.

vocabulary.definition: a letter that isn't a, e, i, o or u
the letters a, e, i, o, u
write the last letter twice before a vowel suffix

emphasize: One short vowel + one consonant at the end → DOUBLE that last consonant before a vowel suffix — to PROTECT the short vowel sound.
The killer contrast: hoping vs hopping — one letter changes everything.
Pre-empt 'runing' (didn't double, so the vowel reads long). Repeated test: 'Short vowel, one consonant on the end? Double it.'

keyConcepts: CVC roots double the final consonant before a vowel suffix
doubling protects the short vowel sound
the hoping/hopping contrast — drop-e vs doubling
misconceptions: not doubling: run + ing → 'runing' (the u would read long, 'roo-ning')
confusing with drop-the-e: writing 'hopeing' or dropping letters from hop
doubling words that shouldn't double (silent-e or long-vowel roots)
hooks: Hoping vs hopping — two words, ONE letter apart, totally different meanings. The double letter is a superhero protecting the short sound.

digital: rule prompt card on screen: 'short vowel + one consonant → double it'

video.watchTask: Every time a word doubles its last letter, shout the twin letters out loud (like 'n-n!') BEFORE the video shows the answer.

afterCheck.question: When do we double the last letter before adding -ing or -ed?
afterCheck.expectedAnswer: When the root ends in one short vowel + one consonant — to protect the short sound

plan.goal: Feel the hoping/hopping contrast — one letter, two meanings — and retrieve the short /o/ sound.
plan.note: Read both words aloud with exaggerated long-o vs short-o; bounce like a bunny on 'hopping'.
plan.successCriteria: Child hears the difference between the long o in hoping and the short o in hopping and can say the short /o/.

script.say: Two words, ONE letter apart, but totally different meanings. Hoping — that's wishing for something. Hopping — that's jumping like a bunny! The only difference is a double p. That little double letter is a superhero — it protects the short sound. Let's learn its trick. Quick — what's the short sound for o? Say the word hop.
script.adaptHints: Listen for /o/ as in hop (short). If shaky: say hot, dog, hop — 'feel that short, sharp /o/? That's the sound we're protecting today.' Bounce on 'hopping' to match the child's energy.

elements.value: the double p protects the short o!

stuckProtocol: If the short /o/ is shaky: say hot, dog, hop together — 'feel that short, sharp /o/?' — before moving on.

plan.goal: Teach the test: ONE short vowel + ONE consonant at the end → double it. Model run → running, hop → hopping; contrast with hope → hoping.
plan.note: Mark the one-vowel-one-consonant pattern under each root before doubling. Put hopping next to hoping and read both.
plan.successCriteria: Child can say the test back: short vowel + one consonant → double it, to protect the short sound.

script.say: Here's the rule. Look at the end of the root. Is it ONE short vowel and then ONE consonant — like r-u-n? If yes, I double that last consonant before a vowel suffix. Watch run: one vowel u, one consonant n → double the n → running. Why? If I wrote runing, the u would go long, like roo-ning. Doubling protects the short /u/. Now hop: one vowel, one consonant → double the p → hopping. Compare hope — that one ends in silent e, so we DROP, not double. Hop → hopping, but hope → hoping.
script.adaptHints: Say the repeated test each time: 'Short vowel + one consonant → double it, to protect the short sound.' Let the child make the 'twin letter' with two fingers.

elements.value: Short vowel + one consonant → double it!

plan.goal: Shared deciding: big + er, sit + ing, swim + ing — the child runs the test out loud, then doubles.
plan.note: Each time, point to the one vowel + one consonant BEFORE doubling. The child says 'double it' before spelling.
plan.successCriteria: Child runs the test unprompted and spells sitting/swimming/bigger correctly.

script.say: You decide with me. Big plus -er. Does it end in one short vowel and one consonant? Say it… so what do we do to the g? … Double it — bigger! Now sit plus -ing… and swim plus -ing. Then read me this pair so I can HEAR the difference: hoping… hopping.
script.adaptHints: If the child forgets the test, tap the last two letters of the root: 'one vowel? one consonant? then…?'

blocks.prompt: Read this pair aloud so I can hear the difference: hoping… hopping.

wrongAnswers.why: didn't double, so the vowel reads long
wrongAnswers.remedy: Read it back — ho-ping? That means wishing! We want bunny-hopping. One vowel, one consonant → double the p.

wrongAnswers.why: confused with drop-e
wrongAnswers.remedy: Does hop have a silent e? No — so we don't drop, we double. hop → hopping.

plan.goal: The key diagnostic: hop + ing. 'hoping' means no doubling; 'hopeing' means rule mix-up with drop-e.
plan.note: After a correct answer, probe WHY we doubled (to keep the short /o/, so it isn't hoping).
plan.successCriteria: Child spells 'hopping' and explains the double p protects the short sound.

script.say: Add -ing to hop. Run the test first — what's on the end of hop?
script.adaptHints: After success, probe: 'Why did we double the p?' Listen for: to keep the short /o/, so it isn't hoping.

blocks.explain: One short vowel + one consonant → double the p: hopping. The twin p's protect the short /o/.

wrongAnswers.why: didn't double, so the vowel reads long — now it means wishing
wrongAnswers.remedy: Read it back — ho-ping? That means wishing! One vowel, one consonant on the end → double the p. Use the rule card.

wrongAnswers.why: confused with the drop-e rule
wrongAnswers.remedy: Does hop have a silent e? No — so we don't drop, we double. hop → hopping.

plan.goal: Independent spelling: -ing/-ed/-er on CVC roots (run, hop, sit, swim, big), doubling the last letter and reading each back.
plan.note: Director draws from practiceBank, start level 2. Keep to CVC roots; the child reads each built word aloud as the self-check.
plan.successCriteria: Child doubles correctly in at least three CVC words and can contrast hoping/hopping.

script.say: Practice time, letter-doubler! I'll send you short, bouncy words. Run the test — one short vowel, one consonant? — make the twin letter, add the tail, and read your new word back to me.
script.adaptHints: Frame the action words around the child's interests (running races, hopping bunnies, swimming lessons) — the spelling words never change.

stuckProtocol: Name why: 'the short sound isn't protected — we need to double.'
Step down: show the rule card and tap the one vowel + one consonant together.
ONE hint: 'what's the last consonant? Make a twin of it.'
Re-ask a smaller version (just double the letter, then add the tail).
Keep it safe: 'The doubling trick takes practice — let's spot the short vowel together.'

plan.goal: Child states the doubling test and why it exists; end on an earned win.
plan.note: Child-led. Optional: play the verified reinforcement video with its watch task if there's appetite.
plan.successCriteria: Child says: short vowel + one consonant at the end → double it, to protect the short sound.

script.say: Tell me the test — when do we double the last letter before adding -ing? … That's it. You tested every word for the short vowel and doubled to protect the sound — and you kept hoping and hopping apart. Brilliant.
script.adaptHints: Process praise the TEST habit (checking the end of the root), not speed. If playing the video, set the watch task first: shout the twin letters before the video does.

wrongAnswers.why: didn't double — the u would read long ('roo-ning')
wrongAnswers.remedy: Read it back — roo-ning? The u went long! What protects the short /u/?

wrongAnswers.why: added an e that was never there
wrongAnswers.remedy: Run has no silent e. Check the end: one vowel, one consonant — what's the move?

hints: Check the end of run: one short vowel, one consonant?
Make a twin of the n, then add -ing.

reteach.say: Run: r-u-n. One short u, one n on the end. The n makes a twin to guard the short sound: run-n-ing. Running!

block.explain: One short vowel + one consonant → double the t: sitting.

wrongAnswers.why: didn't double — the i would read long
wrongAnswers.remedy: Read it — sigh-ting? The i went long! Run the test: what does the t need?

wrongAnswers.why: doubled AND added an e
wrongAnswers.remedy: Great doubling! But no e sneaks in — twin t's, then straight to -ing: sitting.

hints: Say sit — is that vowel short?
Twin t's protect the short i.

reteach.say: Sit: one short i, one t. Double the t — sitt — add -ing: sitting. The twin t's are bodyguards for the short sound.

block.statement: To spell hop + ing, we double the p: hopping.
block.explain: Hop ends in one short vowel + one consonant, so the p doubles: hopping.

wrongAnswers.why: didn't spot the short-vowel + one-consonant pattern
wrongAnswers.remedy: Say hop — short /o/, one p on the end. One vowel, one consonant → what's the move?

hints: Check the end of hop: one vowel? one consonant?
Without the double p it would read ho-ping — wishing!

reteach.say: Hop is a bouncy CVC word: h-o-p. Short o, one p. Double the p so it stays bouncy: hopping. One p would turn it into hoping — a wishing word!

wrongAnswers.why: didn't double — the i would read long
wrongAnswers.remedy: Read it back — swy-ming? Protect that short i. What twin do we need?

wrongAnswers.why: doubled but added a stray e
wrongAnswers.remedy: The twin m's are perfect — but no e! Straight from swimm to -ing: swimming.

hints: Swim ends in one vowel + one consonant.

reteach.say: Swim: short i, one m on the end. The m makes a twin — swimm — then -ing dives in: swimming. Splash!

wrongAnswers.why: didn't double — that's the past of HOPE (wishing), not hop
wrongAnswers.remedy: Read it — hoped means wished! For bunny-jumps we need the twin p's. Run the test on hop.

wrongAnswers.why: lost the suffix's e
wrongAnswers.remedy: Good instinct to change something — but the suffix -ed keeps its e. Twin p's first: hopp + ed.

hints: Same test as -ing: short vowel + one consonant?

reteach.say: The bunny hopped yesterday! Hop: short o, one p → double it → hopp → add -ed → hopped. One p would make hoped — a wish, not a jump.

wrongAnswers.why: didn't double — the i would read long ('by-ger')
wrongAnswers.remedy: Read it back — by-ger? Protect the short i. What does the g need?

wrongAnswers.why: doubled the wrong letter (the suffix's e)
wrongAnswers.remedy: The TWIN is the root's last consonant — the g. Twin g's, then -er: bigger.

hints: -er starts with a vowel, so the same doubling test applies.

reteach.say: Big: one short i, one g. Before -er, the g makes a twin: bigg — bigger! The rule works for -er and -est too: big, bigger, biggest.

practiceBank.skill: choose hoping vs hopping in context

block.prompt: Finish the sentence: 'I was ___ for sunny weather.'
block.explain: Wishing = hoping, from hope (drop the e, one p). Hopping with twin p's is bunny jumps!

wrongAnswers.why: chose the bunny-jump word for a wishing sentence
wrongAnswers.remedy: Read the sentence — is it about jumping or wishing? Which root do we need: hop or hope?

wrongAnswers.why: kept the silent e (Lesson 6 rule slipped)
wrongAnswers.remedy: Hope ends in a silent e — what does the e do before -ing moves in?

hints: Wishing comes from the root hope.
Hope drops its e → one p. Hop doubles → two p's.

reteach.say: Two roots, two rules! Hope (silent e) drops the e → hoping, wishing. Hop (short o) doubles the p → hopping, jumping. The sentence wants wishing — hoping, one p.

wrongAnswers.why: didn't double — the i would read long
wrongAnswers.remedy: Say it — swy-mer? Run the test on swim: one vowel, one consonant → ?

wrongAnswers.why: doubled the wrong letter (the suffix's r)
wrongAnswers.remedy: The twin is the ROOT's last letter, the m. Swimm + er — done.

hints: Same test, new tail: swim ends in one vowel + one m.

reteach.say: A person who swims is a swimmer — twin m's guarding that short i. Swim → swimm → swimmer. A person who runs? Runner — twin n's. The test never changes.

block.prompt: A friend writes: run + ing = runing. Read it back — what goes wrong, and how do we fix it?
block.sample: Without the double n it reads 'roo-ning' — the u goes long. Double the n to protect the short sound: running.

practiceBank.expectedAnswer: The u reads long ('roo-ning'); double the n to protect the short sound — running

wrongAnswers.answer: Nothing went wrong / it looks fine
wrongAnswers.why: shares the didn't-double misconception
wrongAnswers.remedy: Read their word out loud — roo-ning? Is that how run + ing should sound? What protects the short /u/?

wrongAnswers.why: reached for the wrong rule
wrongAnswers.remedy: Is there a silent e on run? No — this is a short-vowel word. What's the doubling test?

hints: Read 'runing' out loud — what happens to the u?
The fix is a twin letter.

reteach.say: Spelling detective time: 'runing' reads roo-ning because nothing is guarding the short u. The fix: double the n — run-n-ing. Short sound safe, word correct: running.

adaptivity.levelUp: 2 consecutive correct at the current level → next level; at level 3, interleave hoping/hopping-style contrasts with -er/-est doublers.
adaptivity.levelDown: 2 misses on the same skill → run the item's reteach with the one-vowel-one-consonant pattern tapped out on the board, then a level-1 item.
adaptivity.masterySignal: 3+ correct across levels 2–3 including one -ed form and the hoping/hopping contrast → mastery ≥ 0.8 for 'double the consonant before a vowel suffix'.
struggleProtocol: Name why: 'the short sound isn't protected — we need to double.'
Step down: show the rule card and tap the one vowel + one consonant together.
ONE hint: 'what's the last consonant? Make a twin of it.'
Re-ask a smaller version (just double the letter, then add the tail), then build back up.
Keep it safe: 'The doubling trick takes practice — let's spot the short vowel together.'
adaptivity.personalization: Frame the action words in the child's world (running at football, hopping like their favourite animal, swimming lessons) — the spelling words never change.
adaptivity.endOnSuccess: Finish on a winnable doubling item; process praise: 'you ran the test on every word and protected every short sound.'

differentiation.support: Keep the on-screen rule card ('short vowel + one consonant → double it') visible at all times; do -ing only at first.
differentiation.stretch: Explain WHY hoping and hopping differ (silent e makes the long sound; doubling protects the short sound), and spell biggest, swimmer.

extension: Find two more CVC words (clap, stop) and double correctly (clapping, stopping).
assessmentEvidence: Child doubles the final consonant correctly in at least three CVC words (running, hopping, sitting) and can contrast hoping/hopping.
revisitLater: Lesson 9's sort mixes doublers with drop-e and y→i. Re-pose hoping vs hopping as a quick retrieval next session.
